The design principles of the Sustainability pillar are:

• Align computational approach to problem complexity: Apply the least resource-intensive approach that satisfies the business requirement. [2][3]
• Minimize the footprint of data and its processing: Retain only data with a defined business purpose, assigning every data set a business owner and an expiration date. [2]
• Maximize utilization: Right-size workloads and implement efficient design to drive high utilization and maximize the energy efficiency of the underlying hardware. [3]
• Anticipate and adopt new, more efficient hardware and software offerings: Support the upstream improvements your partners and suppliers make to help you reduce the impact of your cloud workloads. [3]
• Understand your impact: Measure the impact of your cloud workload and model the future impact of your workload. [4]
• Establish sustainability goals: For each cloud workload, establish long-term sustainability goals such as reducing the compute and storage resources required per transaction. [4]

To manage service quotas, follow these steps:

* Designate a delegated administrator for Service Quotas, typically your central operations or foundation account, to manage quotas across the organization without holding member-account credentials [2].
* Inventory current quota consumption by deploying the Quota Monitor for AWS solution to aggregate quota and usage data from all accounts and Regions, and review initial findings to identify quotas close to their limits, quotas that are likely undersized for current workload trajectories, and quotas that are irrelevant to your workloads [2].
* Establish a baseline quota profile per account type, using different baselines for sandbox, development, and production, and apply the production baseline automatically when an account is marked as production [4].
* Use Service Quotas templates to manage quotas, including quota request templates to new accounts automatically, including accounts vended through AWS Control Tower Account Factory [4].
* Set thresholds well below 100%, with 70-80% being a common starting point, and use the Quota Monitor for AWS solution to track Service Quotas, Trusted Advisor service limits checks, and CloudWatch service metrics across an organization, alerting when consumption approaches configured thresholds [4].
* Review the Service Quotas documentation for each service to understand which limits are adjustable before committing to an architecture that depends on exceeding a default [2].

To choose an AWS Region with sustainability in mind, follow these steps:

* Evaluate essential requirements such as cost, latency, service availability, and compliance [1].
* Consider the carbon intensity of each Region's power grid to make an environmentally conscious decision [1].
* Choose Regions that have both low MBM (Minimum Bearable Maintenance) and low LBM (Lowest Burdened Maintenance) values when business requirements allow [3].
* Review Amazon's carbon free energy projects and their locations, and understand Amazon's renewable energy methodology [3].
* Analyze your workload requirements and constraints, including regulatory and compliance requirements, latency requirements, service and feature availability needs, and cost implications [3].
* Use a decision framework that weighs sustainability alongside other factors, based on your organization's sustainability goals [2].
* Prioritize Regions that have low LBM and MBM for geographically-flexible workloads [2].
* Deploy new workloads according to your Region selection strategy and document the sustainability impact of your Region choices [2].
* Monitor how grid carbon intensity changes over time, using sources such as EPA, AIB, and IEA, and track how your AWS emissions change over time, based on your Regional distribution, in the AWS Sustainability service [2, 4].
* Reassess workload placement as business requirements evolve and update your Region strategy as AWS expands its global infrastructure to new Regions [4].
